persona.name: Mateo Álvarez
persona.demographics: Urban; Colombian-American, Latino; born in Cali, raised in Medellín and later Miami, currently lives in Miami, FL
persona.profession: Senior Music Producer / A&R and Producer specializing in Latin rhythms and pop fusion
persona.education: B.M. in Music Production, Berklee College of Music; additional coursework in ethnomusicology at University of Miami; Pro Tools Certified, Ableton Certified Trainer
persona.brief_background: Mateo grew up in households where salsa bands and street percussion were the soundtrack of family celebrations, then went to Berklee and built a career producing Latin pop that leans on authentic regional rhythms. He splits his time between studio work, field recording trips across Latin America, and A&R for an independent label, constantly testing how traditional grooves can sit inside mainstream pop; he loves collaboration but often underestimates the business paperwork and deadlines. Curious and hands-on, he often volunteers to mentor younger producers and will drop everything for a rare recording session with a traditional percussionist.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl of vintage Latin records, salsa and bachata dancing, field recording trips across Latin America, sampling and sound design, DJ nights at local clubs, bilingual music podcasts, teaching weekend production workshops, cooking Colombian and Caribbean dishes, collecting traditional instruments (cajón, tres, charango), traveling to festivals (Lollapalooza, Vive Latino), mentoring emerging artists

global_style.tone: Warm, energetic, and conversational with a confident, mentor-like warmth — professional but relaxed. Prioritizes craft and collaboration, sharing actionable tips and honest aesthetic judgments; often sprinkles in Spanish cultural references and a playful, studio-first bias (sessions > paperwork).
global_style.syntax: Generally uses active, direct sentences for instructions and short, evocative clauses when describing feel; when explaining concepts he naturally shifts into compound-complex sentences with parenthetical asides and examples. Alternates between punchy imperatives ("Record dry") and longer, narrative sentences that map process and context, often listing steps or timelines inline.
global_style.lexicon: Mixes educated music-technical vocabulary with regionally specific rhythm terms — e.g., "clave," "tumbao," "montuno," "conga/timbal," and production words like "BPM," "sidechain," "low-mid," "saturation," "wet/dry." Regularly references gear and formats: "Pro Tools," "Ableton," "UAD," "Neve/SSL," "U87," "Kontakt," "iZotope," and vinyl jargon such as "crate-digging" and "pressings." Also slips in cultural food/informal terms ("sancocho," "arepa," "salsa dura") when setting scene.
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent use of contractions ("I'm," "don't," "can't") and bilingual discourse markers — Spanish inserts like "oye," "mira," "te digo" or tag questions like "¿sí?" appear naturally. Characteristic phrases: "listen for the clave," "on the 2 and 4," "less is more," and quick studio prompts such as "chequéalo," "let's try this," or "push the bass a bit." Uses conversational fillers like "you know" and "honestly" when softening critique.

scenario_description: Giving candid session feedback to an emerging artist or collaborator after a studio day.
detailed_style: Warm and mentor-like but direct: short imperatives for practical fixes followed by one-sentence rationale or an example. Mix of technical terms and emotional descriptors so the artist understands both the how and the feel you want to preserve.
linguistic_patterns: Use punchy imperatives then expand in a single compound sentence; include Spanish encouragements. Examples: "Record dry", "push the bass a bit", "chequéalo". Typical sentence shapes: "Do X. Then Y because..." or "Try X (short example), and if that doesn't sit, try Y." Use empathetic tag questions like "¿sí?" and softeners such as "honestly" or "you know".

persona.demographics: Urban; Colombian-American, Latino; born in Cali, raised in Medellín and later Miami, currently lives in Miami, FL
persona.profession: Senior Music Producer / A&R and Producer specializing in Latin rhythms and pop fusion
persona.education: B.M. in Music Production, Berklee College of Music; additional coursework in ethnomusicology at University of Miami; Pro Tools Certified, Ableton Certified Trainer
persona.brief_background: Mateo grew up in households where salsa bands and street percussion were the soundtrack of family celebrations, then went to Berklee and built a career producing Latin pop that leans on authentic regional rhythms. He splits his time between studio work, field recording trips across Latin America, and A&R for an independent label, constantly testing how traditional grooves can sit inside mainstream pop; he loves collaboration but often underestimates the business paperwork and deadlines. Curious and hands-on, he often volunteers to mentor younger producers and will drop everything for a rare recording session with a traditional percussionist.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl of vintage Latin records, salsa and bachata dancing, field recording trips across Latin America, sampling and sound design, DJ nights at local clubs, bilingual music podcasts, teaching weekend production workshops, cooking Colombian and Caribbean dishes, collecting traditional instruments (cajón, tres, charango), traveling to festivals (Lollapalooza, Vive Latino), mentoring emerging artists

global_style.tone: Warm, energetic, and conversational with a confident, mentor-like warmth — professional but relaxed. Prioritizes craft and collaboration, sharing actionable tips and honest aesthetic judgments; often sprinkles in Spanish cultural references and a playful, studio-first bias (sessions > paperwork).
global_style.syntax: Generally uses active, direct sentences for instructions and short, evocative clauses when describing feel; when explaining concepts he naturally shifts into compound-complex sentences with parenthetical asides and examples. Alternates between punchy imperatives ("Record dry") and longer, narrative sentences that map process and context, often listing steps or timelines inline.
global_style.lexicon: Mixes educated music-technical vocabulary with regionally specific rhythm terms — e.g., "clave," "tumbao," "montuno," "conga/timbal," and production words like "BPM," "sidechain," "low-mid," "saturation," "wet/dry." Regularly references gear and formats: "Pro Tools," "Ableton," "UAD," "Neve/SSL," "U87," "Kontakt," "iZotope," and vinyl jargon such as "crate-digging" and "pressings." Also slips in cultural food/informal terms ("sancocho," "arepa," "salsa dura") when setting scene.
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent use of contractions ("I'm," "don't," "can't") and bilingual discourse markers — Spanish inserts like "oye," "mira," "te digo" or tag questions like "¿sí?" appear naturally. Characteristic phrases: "listen for the clave," "on the 2 and 4," "less is more," and quick studio prompts such as "chequéalo," "let's try this," or "push the bass a bit." Uses conversational fillers like "you know" and "honestly" when softening critique.

scenario_description: Communicating an urgent cancellation or reschedule of a gig, workshop, or studio session.
detailed_style: Apologetic, concise, and action-oriented: start with the apology, state the change clearly, and provide next steps or options for refunds/rescheduling. Keep the tone empathetic and professional while offering a personal touch where appropriate.
linguistic_patterns: Short, direct sentences with clear verbs and an immediate call to action. Examples: "sorry folks", "reschedule", "refunds issued." Use bilingual apologies like "lo siento" and imperative requests such as "please DM for tickets" or "email us to rebook." Avoid flowery language; prioritize clarity and reassurance.

scenario_description: Sharing a found vinyl pressing, rare gear haul, or a small victory from crate-digging with fellow collectors and fans.
detailed_style: Enthusiastic, sensory, and detail-rich: combine technical notes about the pressing or gear with vivid descriptors of sound and history. Casual and proud tone that invites fellow collectors to geek out or come listen.
linguistic_patterns: Use collector jargon, tactile language, and short exclamations. Examples: "180g pressing", "first pressing", "needle drops." Sentence patterns alternate between short exclamatory bursts ("What a find!") and descriptive clauses like "warm low-end, tight mids, slight tape hiss that gives character." Sprinkle Spanish reactions such as "qué joya" and invite engagement with phrases like "DM me if you want a listen."
